key_insight: The detonation-sprayed FeNiCoMoW coating increased indentation hardness and reduced the retained-depth fraction relative to AISI 321 stainless steel, indicating greater depth recovery during unloading.
engineering_relevance: The coating offers a harder surface, while depth-based indentation descriptors help distinguish retained deformation from unloading recovery.
method: Instrumented Vickers indentation of untreated AISI 321 steel and the FeNiCoMoW coating.
Calculate Martens hardness, residual-depth-based hardness, and retained-depth fraction from load–displacement curves.
Assess coating morphology by optical microscopy and phase composition by X-ray diffraction.
evidence_signal: The continuous coating was 145 ± 8 µm thick; indentation hardness increased from 2.3 ± 0.17 to 8.65 ± 1 GPa, retained-depth fraction decreased from 0.906 to 0.788, and Hpl/HM increased from 1.22 to 1.61.
watch_item: The abstract does not report adhesion, wear, or service-life testing, so higher indentation hardness alone does not establish component durability.
paper_title: Indentation Evaluation of Elastic–Plastic Response and Surface Modifications in Stainless Steel
